phase1.explanation:
This is the moment everything from lesson one becomes real code instead of just an idea.

A [[term:class]] is the blueprint — here, `Student`. It declares what every Student will have: [[term:fields]] like `name`, `age`, and `gpa` to hold data, and [[term:methods]] like `displayInfo()` to define behavior.

An [[term:object]] is an actual instance built from that blueprint — `alice` and `bob` are both Students, but with their own separate values sitting in their own fields.

The [[term:constructor]] is the special method that actually builds a new object: it shares the class's exact name, has no return type at all (not even void), and runs automatically the moment you write `new Student(...)`.

Inside that constructor, you'll almost always see [[term:this]] show up: `this.name = name;` — [[key:this refers to the object currently being built, and it's how Java tells apart the field from the parameter when they share a name]]. Without `this`, Java would have no way to know you meant "assign the parameter to my field" rather than just assigning the parameter to itself.

Once alice and bob exist, you reach their fields and methods with dot notation: `alice.name`, `alice.displayInfo()`. Two objects, same blueprint, completely independent data.

phase2.explanation:
`void Student(...)` looks almost right, but [[warn:that void is exactly what turns this from a constructor into a regular method]]. A real constructor has NO return type at all — not even void — and it must share the class's name exactly.

Because Java now sees `Student(String, int, double)` as a plain method instead of a constructor, the class is left with no matching constructor at all for `new Student("Alice", 20, 3.8)` to call. [[key:The fix is simply removing void]]: `Student(String name, int age, double gpa) { ... }`, with no return type whatsoever.

phase3.openingDialogue: Time to create your first class! The blueprint of the future~ 🏗️

mcq.question:
Which of these is true about a Java constructor?

A) It must have a return type of void
B) It has the same name as the class and no return type at all
C) It can have any name you want
D) It must always take zero parameters

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create a class called Book with:
• Fields: title (String), author (String), pages (int)
• Constructor that initializes all fields
• Method: displayInfo() that prints all book info

In main, create 2 Book objects and call displayInfo() on both.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: if you don't write ANY constructor at all in a class, Java quietly generates a free no-argument one for you behind the scenes, called the default constructor. The moment you write even one constructor yourself, though, Java stops giving you that free one — which is exactly why some classes seem to lose their plain `new ClassName()` option once you add a custom constructor.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thing before you build your next blueprint~
